items.title: 14.3.5 Analytical Expressions of u x v (Determinant formula for u x v)

blocks.text: Let \(\underline{u} = a_1\underline{i} + b_1\underline{j} + c_1\underline{k}\) and \(\underline{v} = a_2\underline{i} + b_2\underline{j} + c_2\underline{k}\), then

by distributive property,
\[= a_1a_2(\underline{i} \times \underline{i}) + a_1b_2(\underline{i} \times \underline{j})\]
\[+ a_1c_2(\underline{i} \times \underline{k}) + b_1a_2(\underline{j} \times \underline{i})\]
\[+ b_1b_2(\underline{j} \times \underline{j}) + b_1c_2(\underline{j} \times \underline{k})\]
\[+ c_1a_2(\underline{k} \times \underline{i}) + c_1b_2(\underline{k} \times \underline{j})\]
\[+ c_1c_2(\underline{k} \times \underline{k})\]

we get
\[= a_1b_2\underline{k} - a_1c_2\underline{j} - b_1a_2\underline{k}\]
\[\quad + b_1c_2\underline{i} + c_1a_2\underline{j} - c_1b_2\underline{i}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How the nine terms became six: the three terms with \(\underline{i} \times \underline{i}\), \(\underline{j} \times \underline{j}\), \(\underline{k} \times \underline{k}\) vanish. Each remaining product is replaced from the cyclic pattern, with a minus sign when the order is against the cycle (e.g. \(\underline{i} \times \underline{k} = -\underline{j}\)).
Then like terms are grouped: the \(\underline{i}\)-terms \(b_1c_2\underline{i} - c_1b_2\underline{i}\), the \(\underline{j}\)-terms \(-a_1c_2\underline{j} + c_1a_2\underline{j} = -(a_1c_2 - c_1a_2)\underline{j}\), and the \(\underline{k}\)-terms \(a_1b_2\underline{k} - b_1a_2\underline{k}\).

The expression of \(3 \times 3\) determinant
\[\begin{vmatrix} \underline{i} & \underline{j} & \underline{k} \\ a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= (b_1c_2 - c_1b_2)\underline{i}\]
\[\quad - (a_1c_2 - c_1a_2)\underline{j}\]
\[\quad + (a_1b_2 - b_1a_2)\underline{k}\]
book_errors: \[\begin{vmatrix} \underline{i} & \underline{j} & \underline{k} \\ a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In this determinant the last entry of the third row is printed as \(c_3\). It must be \(c_2\), the \(z\)-component of \(\underline{v}\); the book prints it correctly in equation (ii) below.
The terms on R.H.S of equation (i) are the same as the terms in the expansion of the above determinant. Hence

blocks.latex: \underline{u} \times \underline{v} = \begin{vmatrix} \underline{i} & \underline{j} & \underline{k} \\ a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \end{vmatrix} \quad \text{(ii)}
blocks.text_alt: u cross v equals the determinant with first row i, j, k, second row a1, b1, c1 and third row a2, b2, c2, equation (ii)

blocks.text: which is known as determinant formula for \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v}\).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The expression on R.H.S. of equation (ii) is not an actual determinant, since its entries are not all scalars. It is simply a way of remembering the complicated expression on R.H.S of equation (i).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to use the determinant formula:
1. Row 1: \(\underline{i}, \underline{j}, \underline{k}\). Row 2: components of the FIRST vector. Row 3: components of the SECOND vector.
2. \(\underline{i}\)-component: hide the \(\underline{i}\) column and cross-multiply what is left.
3. \(\underline{j}\)-component: hide the \(\underline{j}\) column, cross-multiply, and put a MINUS sign in front.
4. \(\underline{k}\)-component: hide the \(\underline{k}\) column and cross-multiply.
Swapping rows 2 and 3 changes the sign of a determinant, which matches \(\underline{v} \times \underline{u} = -\underline{u} \times \underline{v}\).

blocks.title: Example 15
blocks.problem: Find a vector perpendicular to each of the vectors \(\underline{a} = 2\underline{i} - \underline{j} + \underline{k}\) and \(\underline{b} = 4\underline{i} + 2\underline{j} - \underline{k}\).
steps:
Given: \(\underline{a} = 2\underline{i} - \underline{j} + \underline{k}\) and \(\underline{b} = 4\underline{i} + 2\underline{j} - \underline{k}\).
To find: a vector perpendicular to both \(\underline{a}\) and \(\underline{b}\).
Method: by definition, \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b}\) is perpendicular to both \(\underline{a}\) and \(\underline{b}\). So we compute \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b}\) with the determinant formula (ii), then verify with the dot product.

Step 1: Write the determinant
\[\underline{a} \times \underline{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \underline{i} & \underline{j} & \underline{k} \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -1 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: row 2 holds the components of the first vector \(\underline{a}\), row 3 those of the second vector \(\underline{b}\). The order of the rows matters.

Step 2: The \(\underline{i}\)-component (cover the \(\underline{i}\) column)
\[(-1)(-1) - (1)(2) = 1 - 2 = -1\]
Why: cross-multiply the \(2 \times 2\) block left after hiding the first column.

Step 3: The \(\underline{j}\)-component (cover the \(\underline{j}\) column; minus sign)
\[-\big[(2)(-1) - (1)(4)\big]\]
\[= -(-2 - 4) = 6\]
Why: the middle term of a determinant expansion always carries a minus sign.

Step 4: The \(\underline{k}\)-component (cover the \(\underline{k}\) column)
\[(2)(2) - (-1)(4) = 4 + 4 = 8\]
Why: the last \(2 \times 2\) block uses the first two columns.

Step 5: Collect the components
\[\underline{a} \times \underline{b} = -\underline{i} + 6\underline{j} + 8\underline{k}\]
Why: this is the vector the book obtains.

Verification (as in the book): dot product with \(\underline{a}\)
\[\underline{a} \cdot (\underline{a} \times \underline{b})\]
\[= (2\underline{i} - \underline{j} + \underline{k}) \cdot (-\underline{i} + 6\underline{j} + 8\underline{k})\]
\[= (2)(-1) + (-1)(6) + (1)(8)\]
\[= -2 - 6 + 8 = 0\]
Why: a zero dot product means the two vectors are perpendicular.

Check: dot product with \(\underline{b}\)
\[\underline{b} \cdot (\underline{a} \times \underline{b})\]
\[= (4\underline{i} + 2\underline{j} - \underline{k}) \cdot (-\underline{i} + 6\underline{j} + 8\underline{k})\]
\[= (4)(-1) + (2)(6) + (-1)(8)\]
\[= -4 + 12 - 8 = 0\]
Hence \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b}\) is perpendicular to both the vectors \(\underline{a}\) and \(\underline{b}\).
blocks.answer: \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b} = -\underline{i} + 6\underline{j} + 8\underline{k}\) is perpendicular to both \(\underline{a}\) and \(\underline{b}\) (any non-zero multiple of it, e.g. \(\underline{i} - 6\underline{j} - 8\underline{k}\), is also perpendicular to both).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = \begin{vmatrix} \underline{i} & \underline{j} & \underline{k} \\ a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \end{vmatrix}\), first vector in row 2.
2. Expanded: \((b_1c_2 - c_1b_2)\underline{i} - (a_1c_2 - c_1a_2)\underline{j} + (a_1b_2 - b_1a_2)\underline{k}\).
3. The answer is perpendicular to both vectors: check by two dot products equal to zero.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Forgetting the minus sign in front of the \(\underline{j}\)-component.
2. Putting the second vector in row 2: this reverses the sign of the whole answer.
3. Sign slips with negative entries, e.g. \((-1)(-1) = +1\).
